items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Because at that time Jimmy Mundy was writing

ctx.x: Yeah. Well, I mean, all through the '40s these tenors were changing. But the band was playing more and more sort of heavily arranged things.

Yeah. Well, the late '40s, I would say, after Pres went in the Army and he didn't come back, then we had to get musicians -- I think Basie got musicians that were more -- they could read better. They would blend in with the section better. Because at that time Jimmy Mundy was writing and -- let's see, who else was writing? Don Redman did some writing.
And then there were arrangements coming out of the band.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: But before I left the band, James Mundy used to do a lot of writing for the band.

ctx.x: Well, the young arrangers began to appear on the scene like Tad Dameron, Buster Harding…then too, Don Redman used to write quite a bit for the band. And Hugo Winterhalter. But I think Buster Harding did more writing for the band and Eddie Durham used to send some arrangements to the band. But I remember when we opened up in a club called the Royal Roost in New York—that was before Birdland—Tad Dameron made some arrangements for Basie. Basie liked the tune “Good Bait” (sings a little) and Basie told him to make an…

the tables out in the audience. Finally, he just walked up on the bandstand and tore it up. He just wanted something he could understand. At that time, he was very reluctant to some of the new sounds that were by the new arrangers. Because naturally his arrangements were, like Buck…Buck you ought to write for the band.
